blocks.content: Differentiation is the mathematical process we use to find the rate at which one quantity changes with respect to another. As you will come to see, a lot of the time, we will be asking things like: "What is \(\tfrac{dy}{dx}\)?" which is simply asking "how much does the quantity \(y\) change with respect to the quantity \(x\)?"

You’ll also learn how to apply this to a variety of contexts such as speed (mechanics), curve sketching and turning points, and many more real-life situations. But before we dive into what differentiation is and all its cool use cases, we first need to understand the first principles of differentiation.
In general, first principles refers to understanding something from its most basic components and assumptions, which cannot be broken down any further.

So in the context of differentiation, 'first principles' refers to deriving the rules of differentiation from the ground up, using only the definition of a limit. Rather than applying the memorised formulae that we will see in later lessons, for the rest of this lesson we will prove from scratch how the derivative of a function emerges directly from understanding its gradient. With that, let us now switch our focus to gradients!

parts.title: Gradients of Curves and the Tangent Line

blocks.content: Recall that a gradient is a measure of the steepness or slope of a line or surface. It indicates how much a function changes in relation to changes in its input variables. However, as you’ve seen, gradients of curves aren’t constant—for example, consider the following figures:
Figure 1

blocks.alt: A straight line illustrating a constant gradient

blocks.content: Figure 2

blocks.alt: A quadratic curve with a horizontal tangent at its turning point

blocks.content: Figure 3

blocks.alt: A quadratic curve with a non-zero gradient tangent away from the turning point

blocks.content: As you can see in Figure 1, a straight line has constant gradient—no matter where on the curve you are, \(dy/dx\) is the same. But in Figures 2 and 3, the gradient of the quadratic curve changes: at the turning point the tangent is horizontal (gradient 0), while elsewhere it is non-zero.

Since the gradient of the tangent to a curve at a point gives the gradient of the curve at that point, it would be impractical to draw and calculate tangents at every value of \(x\). We need a single expression that tells us the gradient at any point.
That expression is known as the gradient function. In the next part, we will conclude our lesson by deriving this function from first principles.

parts.title: Deriving the Gradient Function from First Principles

blocks.content: To derive the gradient function, imagine a curve with two points, A and B, joined by a chord.

blocks.alt: A curve showing a chord AB between two points

blocks.content: Suppose we wish to find the gradient at A. We draw the chord AB, then move B closer and closer to A. As B approaches A, the gradient of AB approaches the gradient of the curve at A.

blocks.alt: Zoom showing chords approaching the tangent as B moves toward A

blocks.content: Algebraically, let A have coordinates \(\bigl(x,\,f(x)\bigr)\) and B have coordinates \(\bigl(x+h,\,f(x+h)\bigr)\). The gradient of AB is:
$$\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{(x+h)-x} = \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.$$
Taking the limit as \(h\to0\) gives the exact gradient at A:
$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.$$
This is the definition of the derivative from first principles.
Worked Example
Find \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x)=3x^2\) using first principles.
2. Form the difference quotient: $$\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}=\frac{(3x^2+6xh+3h^2)-3x^2}{h}=\frac{6xh+3h^2}{h}=6x+3h.$$
3. Take the limit as \(h\to0\): $$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}(6x+3h)=6x.$$
Thus the derivative of \(3x^2\) is \(6x\). Now practise with the tasks below to solidify your understanding.
